name: cpu-atomic-operation
intent: Express a multi-step mutation of shared state as one indivisible read-modify-write performed by the processor, with an explicit memory-ordering constraint saying how far the compiler and CPU may move the surrounding accesses - so correctness under concurrency rests on a documented guarantee rather than on hope.
problem: Shared state must be read, decided on and written back as a unit, and ordinary loads and stores are not indivisible: a read-modify-write compiled as three instructions can be interleaved between them, and even a single instruction can be reordered with respect to other threads' accesses because the compiler and the CPU both reorder. Using a plain variable or a plain field therefore produces lost updates and visibility bugs that appear rarely, on other hardware, under load. The fix requires knowing which guarantees a platform actually provides - atomically, ordered, or neither.
context: Applies wherever concurrent code shares mutable state whose value depends on more than one field, or where a flag must be published together with the data it describes: reference-counted lifetimes, lock-free stacks and queues, lazy initialisation flags, statistics counters, interrupt-safe flags, state machines with several fields forming an invariant, and the substrate beneath every lock-free structure and software transactional memory. The decision is which ordering each access needs - relaxed, acquire, release, sequentially consistent - and it is the point at which a program's concurrency correctness is decided, since the same code is a data race under one ordering and correct under another.
benefits: Indivisibility by hardware guarantee: the read, the decision and the write become one operation that no other thread can interleave into, which is stronger than any user-space lock it replaces.

Non-blocking progress: a thread that loses a CAS retries or falls back, but no thread ever parks, so a preempted or stalled thread cannot stop the others - the property that makes lock-free structures possible.

Explicit and checkable ordering: naming the memory order documents the required happens-before relationship, and the compiler rejects the mistakes (a release load, a weaker failure order) that produce rare hardware-dependent bugs.
Composite updates become safe: two fields that must change together can be updated as one operation, removing the torn-state class of bug entirely.

The substrate for everything else: lock-free queues, hazard pointers, transactional memory, spinlocks, seqlocks and concurrent map implementations are all built on atomic read-modify-write, so choosing the right primitive is a prerequisite rather than an optimisation.

Cheap where the platform supports it: on x86 a locked read-modify-write is a single instruction, and on weakly-ordered architectures an acquire or release fence is a few extra instructions - usually far cheaper than acquiring a mutex for the same critical section.
tradeoffs: Ordering that is strong enough is easy and ordering that is right is hard: the default (sequentially consistent) is correct but expensive on weak architectures, and a release/acquire downgrade that is too aggressive produces bugs that pass every test and fail in production.

Correctness becomes a whole-program property. The happens-before relation holds only when every participating access participates, so one plain field touched inside an atomic section silently removes the guarantee and no compiler will warn.

Lock-free algorithms are notoriously hard to verify: they rely on helping, descriptors and careful memory orders, and the failure modes (lost updates, double-free, torn pointers) are exactly the ones that reproduce once in a million runs.

Memory-ordering mistakes are the hardest concurrency bugs to find because they are invisible in review, absent under ThreadSanitizer's happens-before analysis unless the access is genuinely non-atomic, and manifest only on hardware with weaker ordering than the developer's.
Unbounded retry loops turn contention into a livelock or a spin-wait that burns a core; backoff is not an optimisation but a correctness requirement for fairness.

Portability is uneven: some types have no lock-free atomic form on some platforms and silently become a mutex-backed operation, turning an intended lock-free structure into a blocking one with no compile-time warning.
Lock-freedom is not wait-freedom, so an individual operation can starve; only the system-level guarantee (some thread makes progress) is typically obtained.
The abstraction is verbose and repetitive at every call site, and the acquire-release discipline around the critical section is easy to get subtly wrong in review.
quality_attributes_note: Performance and scalability are the reason to use atomics at all - a locked instruction is orders of magnitude cheaper than a mutex round trip. Testability and observability are low because a memory-ordering bug is not a test failure: it is a program that passes every test and fails on other hardware, and the race detector only sees non-atomic accesses.

participants.responsibility: The memory word whose read-modify-write is indivisible, carrying the platform's lock-free implementation.
participants.notes: Must be naturally aligned; a misaligned or too-large type may not be lock-free.

participants.responsibility: The indivisible primitive: compare-and-swap replaces the value only if it still matches the expected one, and returns whether it did.
participants.notes: fetch_add and exchange need no comparison and are the cheapest.

participants.role: Memory order (relaxed / acquire / release / acq_rel / seq_cst)
participants.responsibility: Declares how far this access may be reordered with respect to others, and thereby which happens-before edges exist.
participants.notes: The single most consequential decision in concurrent code, and the one hardest to review.

participants.responsibility: Re-reads and tries again when the CAS fails, because another thread won - the CAS is the lock, the loop is the retry.
participants.notes: Needs backoff; unbounded spinning under contention is a livelock.

participants.responsibility: Applies acquire or release ordering to surrounding ordinary accesses when the atomic operation itself does not need the stronger order.
participants.notes: Cheaper than ordering every access, but placement is subtle and platform-specific.

participants.role: Publication protocol (release store / acquire load pair)
participants.responsibility: Ensures data written before a flag is visible to a thread that observes the flag.
participants.notes: The pattern that makes immutable snapshots safely publishable without a lock.

use_cases: Lock-free stacks and queues: the head/tail pointer update is a CAS, and the retry loop is what makes the structure progress without blocking.
Reference counting: an atomic increment/decrement decides whether an object is destroyed, and the ordering is what prevents a use-after-free when the count reaches zero.
Lazy initialisation with a published flag: a release store of the constructed value paired with an acquire load of the flag, instead of double-checked locking with a plain field.
Statistics and metrics counters: fetch_add with relaxed ordering, the common case where only the count matters and no data is published.
Interrupt and signal flags shared between an ISR and the main loop: an atomic store with release, read with acquire, so the ISR's data is visible before the flag is observed.
Memory-ordering publication of immutable state: a reader that acquires a version counter sees a fully constructed snapshot, with no lock on the read path.
Hazard pointers and epoch-based reclamation: the whole reclamation protocol is a CAS loop publishing and clearing a hazard record.
Seqlocks: an odd sequence counter tells readers the data is being written, and the acquire load on the counter is what makes retrying safe.
The commit step of software transactional memory, where read and write sets are installed and validated with acquire/release and CAS.
avoid_when: A mutex is already the right tool and contention is not the bottleneck: a lock is easier to review, blocks rather than spins, and on a low-contention path costs about the same as a locked instruction.
The state is confined to one thread or one core - thread confinement removes the problem entirely and is the cheapest possible answer.
The invariant spans many fields and the update is not naturally one read-modify-write: use a lock, a double-buffer with an atomic swap, or an immutable snapshot plus an atomic pointer.
A higher-level abstraction already provides it: a BlockingQueue, a concurrent map, or a channel gives correctness without anyone reasoning about memory order.

The platform lacks a lock-free atomic for the type: check is_lock_free, because a silently mutex-backed atomic reintroduces blocking and hides the fact that the design's progress guarantee does not hold.
Blocking work must happen while holding the state: an atomic cannot make an I/O call atomic, and holding a spin lock across a syscall is a disaster on a preemptive scheduler.
You cannot state the required ordering: if nobody can say which happens-before edge the code needs, the code should not be using atomics - the pattern's value is entirely in the correctness argument.
pitfalls: The torn-invariant bug: two fields updated by two separate atomics, each individually correct, so a reader can see the intermediate state. The update must be one operation, or published as an immutable snapshot.

Ordering that is too weak: a relaxed access to what is meant to publish data, which works on x86 and fails on ARM - the classic portability bug that only appears on the developer's weaker-ordered hardware in production.

The failure-order mistake: the failure memory order of a CAS may not be stronger than the success order and may not be acquire/release when the success order was, and the compiler enforces this - read the diagnostic rather than working around it.
compare_exchange_weak in a loop with a recomputed expectation: weak CAS may fail spuriously, so the loop must re-read the value each iteration rather than retrying with a stale expectation.

Spinning without backoff: under contention a retry loop burns a core and can livelock, because the loser never gets scheduled while the winner keeps winning. Add a pause/yield and exponential backoff.
A plain field read inside an atomic critical section: it participates in no happens-before relation, so the atomic discipline is silently void for that access.
Unaligned or too-wide atomics: an atomic wider than the platform supports is not lock-free and may be emulated, so the intended progress guarantee does not hold.
Assuming a fence is as strong as an ordering on the access: an acquire fence after a relaxed load is close, but the exact rules are subtle and mixing them is how subtle bugs are made.

related_patterns_notes.lock-free-programming: The application on top of the substrate. cpu-atomic-operation is the single indivisible instruction and its ordering contract; lock-free-programming is the discipline of building multi-step non-blocking algorithms (progress guarantees, ABA, reclamation, helping) out of them. One is a machine primitive, the other is a method.
related_patterns_notes.lock-free-queue: The best-known consumer. The Michael-Scott queue is CAS and a retry loop at each of head and tail, plus a memory-management scheme for the removed node - which is exactly why this record names hazard pointers and epoch reclamation as the things built on top.
related_patterns_notes.software-transactional-memory: Records a read set and a write set and installs a transaction descriptor with a multi-word CAS; the atomic operation is what makes the commit atomic and the validation meaningful.
related_patterns_notes.double-checked-locking: Historically implemented with a plain field and a volatile flag, which is broken because the object's construction writes are not ordered against the flag read. The correct version uses atomics on both, or a static initialiser.
related_patterns_notes.copy-and-swap: Note the two different senses of the same words: this catalog's copy-and-swap is the exception-safety idiom (build a temporary, commit with operations that cannot fail), not the CPU primitive. They are unrelated patterns that happen to share a name.
related_patterns_notes.thread-confinement: The best optimisation: if no reference to the state escapes the owning thread, there is nothing to make atomic. Confinement eliminates the problem rather than solving it.
related_patterns_notes.read-write-lock: A mutex family with its own atomic substrate and its own problem (writer starvation). Reach for atomics directly when the critical section is a few instructions, and for a read-write lock when it is not.
related_patterns_notes.immutability: The complementary strategy. With immutable data the only shared write is a pointer store, which needs one release store and one acquire load - and everything else can be relaxed or non-atomic.
related_patterns_notes.scope-guard: The RAII wrapper that must be used for every lock or fence whose release must happen on every path, including unwinding; the atomics record's release ordering is what a correctly-ordered scope guard establishes.
related_patterns_notes.dirty-flag: A dirty flag is a plain boolean set when state changes and cleared when saved. Written that way it is a data race, and the correct version makes the flag an atomic store with release ordering so a reader that observes it also observes the data it describes - the publication protocol this record describes, in its most common concrete form.
related_patterns_notes.copy-on-write: The strategy that minimises how many atomics a program needs. With copy-on-write, the only shared write is a pointer store, so one release store and one acquire load carry the whole update and everything the old value contained needs no synchronisation at all.

anti_patterns: Using relaxed ordering for an access that publishes data, because it worked on the development machine's strongly-ordered architecture.
Building a multi-field invariant out of several individually atomic updates, on the assumption that atomic means transaction.
Retrying a failed CAS in a tight loop with no backoff, turning contention into a livelock that burns a core.
Using a strong ordering everywhere for convenience, paying the fence cost on every access and obscuring which orderings the algorithm actually depends on.
Handing an atomic to a type the platform does not implement lock-free and assuming the progress guarantee - check is_lock_free rather than assume.
Holding a spin lock across a syscall, a page fault or an allocation, so a preemption becomes a system-wide stall.
A plain (non-atomic) read of a field inside an atomic critical section, silently removing the happens-before edge the protocol needed.
Mixing an acquire-release protocol with a plain-field fast path that reads the same data - the fast path is the bug, and it is the one that is faster.
design_principles: Name the ordering: the memory order is a specification of the happens-before edge, not a tuning knob. If you cannot say which edge it establishes, do not weaken it.
One indivisible operation per invariant: if the update must be seen as a unit, it must be one read-modify-write or one atomic publication of an immutable value.
Prefer publication to mutation: write the data first, then release-publish the pointer, so readers need only acquire and the rest of the code can stay plain.
Progress is a design goal: choose retry with backoff over parking, and prefer the strongest guarantee you can actually implement.
Readiness is not invisibility: verify the platform supports the operation lock-free before relying on the guarantee.
best_practices: Start at sequentially consistent and weaken only with a written reason; downgrading is a mechanical change but proving it correct is not.
Keep the acquire-release pair symmetric: a release store paired with an acquire load, both naming the same variable, and document the edge in a comment.
Add pause/yield or exponential backoff to every CAS retry loop, and bound it if fairness matters.
Check is_lock_free for the type in question at the sizes you use, and assert it in a test if the progress guarantee matters.
Publish immutable state and store only the pointer, so the read path is a single acquire load and the payload needs no synchronisation at all.
Run tests under ThreadSanitizer and on a weakly-ordered target (ARM) - TSan catches non-atomic accesses, not ordering mistakes, and the ordering mistakes only show on the other architecture.
Document the progress guarantee the algorithm claims (lock-free, wait-free, obstruction-free) in the type or module header, because the difference is invisible at the call site.
Keep atomics out of the layer that does not need them: confine state where you can, and let one layer own the synchronisation.
Never hold a spin lock across a syscall, allocation, or anything that can block or be preempted.
When a field must be published with data, publish the data pointer first and the flag second; the reverse order publishes a half-built object.
sources: cppreference.com, 'std::memory_order' - the normative meaning of relaxed, consume, acquire, release, acq_rel and seq_cst, the release-acquire synchronises-with relation, the release sequence, and the note that sequential consistency is invalidated by weaker orderings. https://cppreference.dev/w/cpp/atomic/memory_order

LLVM, 'Atomic Instructions and Concurrency Guide' - how the orderings map to IR and to machine instructions, the six levels of atomicity, the fence semantics, and the per-architecture codegen (x86 MOV/XCHG/LOCK CMPXCHG/MFENCE versus ARM LDREX/STREX with barriers). https://llvm.org/docs/Atomics.html

David Herlihy and Nathaniel Lin (The Rustonomicon), 'Atomics' - the acquire-release and relaxed disciplines with a worked spinlock, the happens-before reasoning, and the explicit warning that sequential consistency is the right choice when you are not yet confident about the weaker orderings. https://doc.rust-lang.org/nomicon/atomics.html

Boehm and Adve, 'Foundations of the C++ Concurrency Memory Model' (PLDI 2008), as cited by the Go memory model - the release/acquire framework that the C11, C++11, Java, Rust and Swift models all inherit. https://go.dev/ref/mem

Timothy Chan and Tomer shalom, 'Scalable FIFO Channels for Programming via Communicating Sequential Processes' (Euro-Par 2019) - the practical consequence of atomics in a real primitive: how relaxed operations, fences and descriptors are combined to build a non-blocking channel on which a progress guarantee can still be claimed. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1007/978-3-030-29400-7_23
